source: Lecture: Visual System slides 6-9
question: A neurophysiologist records electrical activity from successive cell layers of the neural retina while flashing light onto the photoreceptors. Which cell type is the first in the visual pathway to generate action potentials?

options.text: Cone photoreceptors
Retinal ganglion cells
Retinal pigment epithelial cells
Bipolar cells
Rod photoreceptors

explanation: Photoreceptors (1st order) and bipolar cells (2nd order) signal with graded potentials only. Retinal ganglion cells (3rd order) are the first neurons to generate action potentials; their central processes form the optic nerve, optic chiasm, and optic tract. The RPE is a supporting (non-neural) layer.
high_yield_pearl: Rods/cones → bipolar cells (graded potentials) → ganglion cells (first action potentials; axons = optic nerve).

source: Lecture: Visual System slide 7
question: In complete darkness, a rod photoreceptor is tonically depolarized. A brief flash of light is then directed onto this rod. Which change in the rod is most likely to occur?

options.text: Generation of an all-or-none action potential
Depolarization with increased glutamate release
Opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels in its axon
Hyperpolarization of the photoreceptor membrane
No change until the ganglion cell fires

explanation: Photoreceptors are depolarized in the dark (the 'dark current'). Light closes cGMP-gated cation channels, hyperpolarizing the cell and reducing glutamate release onto bipolar cells. Photoreceptors never fire action potentials.
high_yield_pearl: Photoreceptors are normally depolarized; light HYPERPOLARIZES them.

source: Content Q4: Properties of photoreceptors
question: A 34-year-old man says he sees well during the day but has great difficulty walking through a dimly lit parking lot at night. Visual acuity and color discrimination are normal. Dysfunction of which retinal cells best explains his symptoms?

options.text: Rods located mainly in the peripheral retina
Ganglion cells exiting at the optic disc
Bipolar cells located only in the macula
Cones concentrated within the fovea
Relay neurons of the lateral geniculate

explanation: Rods are highly light-sensitive (dim light), mediate black-and-white vision, have low acuity, contain rhodopsin, and predominate in the peripheral retina. Cones mediate bright-light, color, high-acuity vision and are concentrated in the fovea; normal acuity and color vision indicate intact cones.
high_yield_pearl: Rods: dim light, B&W, low acuity, periphery, rhodopsin. Cones: bright light, color, high acuity, fovea, cone opsins.

source: Content Q5: Vitamin A and photoreceptors
question: A 6-year-old child from a region with severe food insecurity is brought for evaluation because he cannot see after sunset. Examination shows dry, roughened conjunctivae. Deficiency of the responsible nutrient most directly impairs which process?

options.text: Secretion of aqueous humor by the ciliary body
Myelination of the optic nerve axons
Contraction of the ciliary muscle for near vision
Glutamate release from retinal bipolar cells
Synthesis of rhodopsin and cone opsin pigments

explanation: Vitamin A (retinal) is required for synthesis of rhodopsin (rods) and cone opsins. Because rods depend on rhodopsin for dim-light vision, night blindness is the earliest symptom; xerophthalmia (dry conjunctiva) follows.
high_yield_pearl: Vitamin A → retinal → rhodopsin; deficiency causes night blindness first.

source: Content Q3: Optic disc, macula, fovea
question: During a fundoscopic exam, a student is asked to identify the small central pit within the macula that contains almost exclusively cones and provides the highest visual acuity. Which structure is being described?

options.text: Optic disc
Ora serrata
Fovea
Ciliary body
Peripheral retina

explanation: The fovea is the point of highest visual acuity and contains mostly cones. The macula is the region surrounding the fovea. The optic disc is where ganglion cell axons exit (the physiologic blind spot).
high_yield_pearl: Fovea = highest acuity, mostly cones; macula surrounds it; optic disc = blind spot.

source: Content Q3: Optic disc
question: During confrontation testing of one eye, a small target disappears when it is about 15 degrees temporal to the point of fixation and reappears when moved slightly farther. This normal finding corresponds to which retinal region?

options.text: Fovea, where cones are most densely packed
Macula, the region surrounding the fovea
Ciliary body, where aqueous is secreted
Optic disc, where ganglion cell axons exit the eye
Peripheral retina, where rods predominate

explanation: The optic disc has no photoreceptors because it is where retinal ganglion cell axons leave the eye to form the optic nerve, creating the physiologic blind spot in the temporal visual field of each eye.
high_yield_pearl: No photoreceptors at the optic disc → physiologic blind spot (temporal field).

source: Content Q1: Refractive conditions table
question: A 12-year-old girl has difficulty reading the whiteboard from the back of her classroom but reads books held close without difficulty. Refraction shows that parallel light rays come to focus in front of the retina. What is the most likely structural cause?

options.text: The axial length of the eye is too short
The cornea has unequal curvature
The axial length of the eye is too long
The ciliary muscle is paralyzed
The lens has stiffened with age

explanation: Myopia (nearsightedness): image focused in front of the retina because the eye is too long. Hyperopia: focused behind the retina, eye too short. Astigmatism: unfocused image from irregular corneal curvature. Presbyopia: image behind the retina because the lens becomes stiff with age.
high_yield_pearl: Myopia = eye too long (focus in front). Hyperopia = eye too short (focus behind).

source: Content Q1: Refractive conditions table
question: A 7-year-old boy fails a near-vision screening but sees distant objects clearly. His lens is soft and flexible. Retinoscopy shows that images come to focus behind the retina. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The axial length of the eye is too short
The axial length of the eye is too long
The cornea has unequal curvature
The retina has separated from the RPE
The lens proteins have denatured

explanation: Hyperopia (farsightedness) occurs when the eye is too short, so images focus behind the retina. Unlike presbyopia, it is not due to lens stiffening (this child's lens is flexible). Hyperopic adults are also at increased risk for acute angle-closure glaucoma.
high_yield_pearl: Hyperopia = short eye; hyperopes are at risk for angle-closure glaucoma.

source: Content Q1: Refractive conditions table
question: A 26-year-old man complains of blurry vision at all distances. On a chart of radiating lines, the vertical lines appear sharp while the horizontal lines appear blurred. Which abnormality best explains these findings?

options.text: Opacification of the lens nucleus
Loss of lens elasticity with age
Excessive axial length of the globe
Insufficient axial length of the globe
Unequal curvature of the cornea

explanation: Astigmatism results from unequal curvature of the cornea in different meridians, producing an unfocused image so that lines in one orientation appear sharper than lines in another.
high_yield_pearl: Astigmatism = irregular corneal curvature → unfocused image.

source: Content Q1: Refractive conditions table
question: A 47-year-old accountant who has never needed glasses now holds restaurant menus at arm's length to read them. Distance vision remains normal. Which change best explains her new difficulty?

options.text: Paralysis of the ciliary muscle from CN III injury
Age-related stiffening of the lens limits rounding
Progressive elongation of the globe
Development of irregular corneal curvature
Clouding of the lens from denatured proteins

explanation: Presbyopia: with age the lens becomes stiff and cannot round up adequately during accommodation, so near images focus behind the retina. Cataract (denatured lens proteins) causes clouding and glare rather than isolated loss of near focus.
high_yield_pearl: Presbyopia = stiff lens with age → near image focused behind retina.

source: Content Q2: Aqueous humor production and flow
question: Which sequence correctly describes the production and flow of aqueous humor in the eye?

options.text: Choroid plexus → vitreous chamber → posterior chamber → pupil → optic disc
Ciliary body → anterior chamber → pupil → posterior chamber → vitreous body
Trabecular meshwork → anterior chamber → pupil → posterior chamber → ciliary body
Ciliary body → posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork
Lacrimal gland → anterior chamber → pupil → posterior chamber → Schlemm canal

explanation: Aqueous humor is secreted by the ciliary body into the posterior chamber, passes through the pupil into the anterior chamber, and drains through the trabecular meshwork at the iridocorneal angle into the canal of Schlemm. Glaucoma is fundamentally a drainage problem.
high_yield_pearl: Ciliary body (makes) → posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork (drains).

source: Content Q6: Order of visual structures
question: Visual signals travel from the retina to the visual cortex through a defined series of structures. Which structure lies immediately between the optic tract and the optic radiations?

options.text: Primary visual cortex
Superior colliculus
Lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
Pretectal nucleus
Optic chiasm

explanation: Order: retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus (4th-order neurons) → optic radiations (geniculocalcarine fibers) → visual cortex. The pretectal nucleus receives light-reflex fibers that bypass the LGN.
high_yield_pearl: Retina → ON → chiasm → OT → LGN → optic radiations → visual cortex.

source: Content Q9: First place a lesion affects both eyes
question: Moving from the eye toward the brain, what is the most anterior location in the visual pathway at which a single lesion can produce visual field deficits in BOTH eyes?

options.text: Optic chiasm
Optic disc
Retina
Intracanalicular optic nerve
Intraorbital optic nerve

explanation: Lesions of the retina or anywhere along the optic nerve produce monocular deficits. The optic chiasm is the first site where fibers from both eyes are together (nasal fibers cross), so it is the first location where a lesion affects the fields of both eyes.
high_yield_pearl: Anterior to the chiasm = monocular; chiasm and beyond = both eyes.

source: Case 2: Visual pathway (car accidents)
question: A 50-year-old man is brought to the clinic by a friend who says he has had several car accidents over the past few months. He denies any eye pain. The results of visual field testing are shown. Which fibers are most likely interrupted?

options.text: All fibers of the right optic nerve
Crossing fibers from both nasal hemiretinas
Inferior retinal fibers in Meyer's loop
Superior retinal fibers in the parietal lobe
Uncrossed fibers from both temporal hemiretinas

explanation: The figure shows bitemporal hemianopia (loss of both temporal fields, 'tunnel vision'). Temporal visual fields are seen by the nasal hemiretinas, whose fibers cross in the optic chiasm. Loss of peripheral vision makes driving dangerous.
high_yield_pearl: Bitemporal hemianopia = crossing nasal fibers at the optic chiasm.

source: Case 2: Visual pathway (pituitary)
question: Imaging of the patient with bitemporal hemianopia reveals a slowly enlarging mass compressing the optic chiasm from below. The mass most likely arises from which structure?

options.text: Uncus of the medial temporal lobe
Pineal gland above the superior colliculi
Cavernous sinus lateral to the sella
Lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
Pituitary gland within the sella turcica

explanation: The pituitary gland sits immediately below the optic chiasm in the sella turcica. Expanding pituitary adenomas compress the crossing nasal fibers, causing bitemporal hemianopia. Pineal tumors compress the posterior commissure (vertical gaze palsy).
high_yield_pearl: Pituitary adenoma → chiasm compression → bitemporal hemianopia.

source: Lecture: Visual Field slides 23-24
question: A patient with both eyes open fixates on a central point while a light stimulus is presented in the right visual hemifield. Which retinal halves receive this stimulus?

options.text: Both temporal hemiretinas
Right temporal and left nasal hemiretinas
Right superior and left inferior hemiretinas
Both nasal hemiretinas
Right nasal and left temporal hemiretinas

explanation: Images are inverted and reversed by the lens. Light from the right visual field strikes the nasal retina of the right eye and the temporal retina of the left eye. Each half of the retina receives information from the opposite visual hemifield.
high_yield_pearl: Nasal retina sees the temporal field; temporal retina sees the nasal field.

source: Case 3: Monocular central vision loss
question: A 62-year-old woman reports painless difficulty seeing that has progressed over the past year. There is no history of trauma. Examination shows central visual loss in the right eye; the left eye is entirely normal. Where is the lesion most likely located?

options.text: Right eye or right optic nerve, anterior to the chiasm
Right occipital pole of the cortex
Left optic tract near the LGN
Right lateral geniculate nucleus
Optic chiasm at the midline

explanation: A deficit confined to one eye is a monocular deficit, so the lesion must lie anterior to the optic chiasm—within the right eye itself or along the right optic nerve. Lesions at or behind the chiasm affect the fields of both eyes.
high_yield_pearl: Monocular deficit → lesion in that eye or its optic nerve.

source: Lecture: Visual System Damage slide 26
question: A 31-year-old man sustains a penetrating injury to the right orbit in a workplace accident. Visual field testing performed after he is stabilized is shown. Which structure has been damaged?

options.text: Optic chiasm
Left optic tract
Left optic nerve
Right optic nerve
Right optic tract

explanation: The figure shows complete loss of vision in the right eye only (unilateral anopia), with a normal left field. This monocular blindness localizes to the right optic nerve (or the right eye). Optic tract lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
high_yield_pearl: Complete monocular blindness = ipsilateral optic nerve.

source: Content Q9-10: Naming field deficits
question: A 66-year-old man is evaluated after the sudden onset of visual difficulty. Visual field testing is shown; the central (macular) field is also lost. A single lesion in which location best explains this pattern?

options.text: Left optic nerve
Right optic tract
Left optic tract
Optic chiasm
Left Meyer's loop

explanation: The figure shows right homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing. This results from a lesion of the left optic tract, left LGN, or all of the left optic radiations. Macular sparing would suggest a visual cortex (PCA) lesion. Meyer's loop lesions cause only a superior quadrantanopia.
high_yield_pearl: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia = optic tract, LGN, or all optic radiations.

source: Case 1: Bumping head on upper cabinets
question: A 30-year-old executive visits her physician because of a painful bump on her head. She has repeatedly hit her head on the upper cabinets in her kitchen. Results of her ocular examination are shown. Where is the lesion most likely located?

options.text: Left parietal lobe (dorsal loop)
Left temporal lobe (Meyer's loop)
Optic chiasm
Right temporal lobe (Meyer's loop)
Left cuneus

explanation: The figure shows right superior (upper) homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky'). Meyer's loop carries fibers from the inferior retina of the opposite visual field through the temporal lobe; because images are inverted, the inferior retina sees the superior field. A left lingual gyrus lesion could produce the same deficit (possibly with macular sparing).
high_yield_pearl: Pie in the sky = contralateral Meyer's loop (temporal lobe) or lingual gyrus.

source: Lecture slide 18-20: Optic radiations
question: Optic radiation fibers in Meyer's loop sweep anteriorly through the temporal lobe before reaching the occipital lobe. These fibers carry information from which part of the retina, and where do they terminate?

options.text: Nasal retina only; superior colliculus of the midbrain
Inferior retina; cuneus above the calcarine sulcus
Superior retina; lingual gyrus below the calcarine sulcus
Inferior retina; lingual gyrus below the calcarine sulcus
Superior retina; cuneus above the calcarine sulcus

explanation: Inferior fibers (Meyer's loop) carry the inferior retina (superior visual field) through the temporal lobe to the lingual gyrus. Superior fibers (dorsal loop) carry the superior retina (inferior visual field) through the parietal lobe to the cuneus.
high_yield_pearl: Meyer's loop: inferior retina → temporal lobe → lingual gyrus (sees the UPPER field).

source: Case 1: Vascular supply
question: If the right superior homonymous quadrantanopia in the woman who bumps her head had appeared suddenly from an infarct of the left Meyer's loop, which artery would most likely be occluded?

options.text: Middle cerebral artery
Posterior cerebral artery
Anterior communicating artery
Anterior cerebral artery
Ophthalmic artery

explanation: Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe is supplied mainly by branches of the middle cerebral artery. An infarct of the lingual gyrus (which could produce the same field cut) would instead involve the posterior cerebral artery.
high_yield_pearl: Meyer's loop → MCA; lingual gyrus/cuneus → PCA.

source: Case 4: Tripping over the dog on the right
question: A 24-year-old man sees a neurologist because he keeps tripping over his dog, especially when the dog is on his right side. Visual field testing is shown. Where is the lesion most likely located?

options.text: Right parietal lobe optic radiations (dorsal loop)
Right cuneus above the calcarine sulcus
Left parietal lobe optic radiations (dorsal loop)
Left lingual gyrus below the calcarine sulcus
Left temporal lobe optic radiations (Meyer's loop)

explanation: The figure shows right inferior (lower) homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor'). Superior optic radiation fibers (dorsal loop) carry the superior retina, which sees the inferior field, through the parietal lobe to the cuneus. A left-sided lesion affects the right field.
high_yield_pearl: Pie on the floor = contralateral parietal radiations or cuneus.

source: Case 4: Parietal white matter lesion
question: An MRI at the level of the parietal lobe shows a lesion in the left parietal white matter. Depending on how deeply it extends into the optic radiations, which pair of visual field deficits could this lesion produce?

options.text: Bitemporal hemianopia or right monocular blindness
Right superior or right inferior quadrantanopia
Right superior quadrantanopia or right homonymous hemianopia
Left inferior quadrantanopia or left homonymous hemianopia
Right inferior quadrantanopia or right homonymous hemianopia

explanation: A parietal lesion first interrupts the superior (dorsal loop) radiations, causing right inferior quadrantanopia; deeper extension can interrupt all the radiations, causing right homonymous hemianopia. At the parietal level it would not be expected to involve only the inferior (Meyer's loop) fibers.
high_yield_pearl: Parietal radiations carry the inferior visual field; deep lesions → full hemianopia.

source: Content Q10: Hemianopia with macular sparing
question: A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has a sudden change in vision. Visual field testing is shown. Occlusion of which artery is most likely responsible?

options.text: Left anterior cerebral artery
Left posterior cerebral artery
Right posterior cerebral artery
Left ophthalmic artery
Left middle cerebral artery

explanation: The figure shows right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, characteristic of an infarct of the left visual cortex (cuneus and lingual gyrus) supplied by the left PCA. The macular cortex is spared because of its large territory and collateral MCA supply.
high_yield_pearl: Homonymous hemianopia WITH macular sparing → contralateral PCA infarct of visual cortex.

source: Content Q7: Macular sparing
question: Which feature best explains why central (macular) vision is often preserved after an occipital infarct?

options.text: Macular information is processed in the colliculi
Macular fibers cross in the posterior commissure
Macular fibers travel only within Meyer's loop
Macular fibers bypass the LGN to reach the cortex
Macular cortex is large and has dual (PCA and MCA) supply

explanation: The cortical representation of the macula at the occipital pole is large (similar to the hand and face on the postcentral gyrus) and receives blood from two vessels (PCA and MCA), so it is typically spared in infarcts. Large lesions from other causes (e.g., trauma) may not spare it.
high_yield_pearl: Macular sparing = large cortical territory + dual blood supply; seen with infarcts, not always with trauma.

source: Content Q7 / VisRef Case 3: Trauma without macular sparing
question: A 25-year-old man falls backward from a truck and strikes his occiput on the pavement. CT shows extensive bilateral destruction of the occipital lobes. He has complete loss of vision in both eyes without macular sparing. Why is macular sparing absent?

options.text: Dual macular blood supply is present only in children
The lesion spared the lateral geniculate nucleus
Trauma destroyed the occipital pole regardless of blood supply
Trauma interrupted the pupillary light pathway
Macular sparing only occurs with optic tract lesions

explanation: Macular sparing depends on the dual vascular supply protecting the macular cortex during infarcts. A large traumatic lesion destroys the macular cortex directly, so central vision is lost as well. The pupillary light reflex remains intact because it does not depend on the cortex.
high_yield_pearl: Large traumatic occipital lesions can cause complete blindness without macular sparing.

source: Content Q8: Agnosia
question: Two weeks after a stroke, a 68-year-old woman can describe the shape, color, and size of a key placed in front of her but cannot say what it is. When the key is placed in her hand, she immediately names it. Which deficit best describes her condition?

options.text: Visual agnosia from damage to visual association cortex
Bitemporal hemianopia from a chiasmal lesion
Cortical blindness from destruction of primary visual cortex
Bilateral optic neuropathy with loss of acuity
Gaze palsy from a frontal eye field lesion

explanation: Agnosia is a cognitive deficit in which perception is intact but neighboring association cortex cannot interpret the sensory information. She can see the object (primary visual cortex intact) but cannot recognize it visually, while tactile recognition is preserved.
high_yield_pearl: Agnosia = perception intact, interpretation lost (e.g., astereognosis, visual object agnosia).

source: Content Q11: Role of the colliculi
question: A sudden flash of light in a patient's peripheral visual field causes an immediate, reflexive turning of the head and eyes toward the stimulus. Which structure is most directly responsible for this orienting reflex?

options.text: Inferior colliculus
Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Lateral geniculate nucleus
Superior colliculus
Lingual gyrus

explanation: The superior colliculi mediate reflexive head and eye turning toward visual stimuli. The inferior colliculi serve the same orienting role for auditory stimuli. The LGN relays conscious vision to the cortex.
high_yield_pearl: Superior colliculus = orient to visual stimuli; inferior colliculus = orient to sounds.

source: Content Q11: Role of the colliculi
question: While sitting in a quiet room, a student hears a book drop loudly behind and to his left, and reflexively turns his head and eyes toward the sound. Which midbrain structure is most important for this reflex?

options.text: Pretectal nucleus
Inferior colliculus
Lateral geniculate nucleus
Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Superior colliculus

explanation: The inferior colliculi are important for reflexive head and eye turning toward auditory stimuli, whereas the superior colliculi perform this role for visual stimuli. The pretectal and Edinger-Westphal nuclei mediate pupillary reflexes.
high_yield_pearl: Auditory orienting reflex → inferior colliculus.

source: Lecture slides 22-24: Optic tract composition
question: The right optic tract contains axons from which hemiretinas, and which visual field do these fibers represent?

options.text: Right temporal and left nasal hemiretinas; left visual field
Right temporal and left nasal hemiretinas; right visual field
Right nasal and left temporal hemiretinas; right visual field
Both nasal hemiretinas; both temporal visual fields
Right nasal and right temporal hemiretinas; entire right eye field

explanation: After the chiasm, each optic tract carries ipsilateral temporal (uncrossed) and contralateral nasal (crossed) fibers. The right temporal retina and left nasal retina both see the LEFT visual field, so a right optic tract lesion causes left homonymous hemianopia.
high_yield_pearl: Right optic tract = left visual field (right temporal + left nasal retina).

source: Lecture slide 20-21: Cuneus
question: A small infarct is confined to the right cuneus, above the calcarine sulcus. Which visual field deficit is most likely?

options.text: Right inferior homonymous quadrantanopia
Right superior homonymous quadrantanopia
Left superior homonymous quadrantanopia
Left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia
Bitemporal hemianopia

explanation: The cuneus receives the dorsal-loop fibers carrying the superior retina, which sees the inferior visual field. A right-sided lesion affects the left visual field, producing left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia (often with macular sparing if from a PCA infarct).
high_yield_pearl: Cuneus = inferior field; lingual gyrus = superior field (both contralateral).

source: Lecture slide 23: Inversion of images
question: Because images are inverted as they pass through the lens, light from an object located in the inferior visual field falls on which part of the retina?

options.text: Optic disc
Nasal retina only
Inferior retina
Temporal retina only
Superior retina

explanation: The lens inverts images upside down and reverses them left to right. Objects in the inferior visual field are imaged on the superior retina, whose fibers travel in the dorsal (parietal) loop to the cuneus.
high_yield_pearl: Inferior visual field → superior retina → dorsal loop → cuneus.

source: Integration: LGN lesion and light reflex
question: A 59-year-old woman has a small hemorrhage confined to the left lateral geniculate nucleus. Which combination of findings is most likely?

options.text: Right homonymous hemianopia with an absent consensual reflex
Right homonymous hemianopia with normal pupillary light reflexes
Left homonymous hemianopia with normal pupillary light reflexes
Bitemporal hemianopia with normal pupillary light reflexes
Right monocular blindness with an afferent pupillary defect

explanation: The left LGN relays the right visual field, so a lesion causes right homonymous hemianopia. Pupillary light reflex fibers leave the optic tract before the LGN (via the brachium of the superior colliculus to the pretectal nucleus), so pupillary reflexes are normal.
high_yield_pearl: Light-reflex fibers bypass the LGN, so LGN lesions spare pupillary reflexes.

source: Lecture slide 25 speaker notes: Clinical significance
question: Visual field deficits often develop slowly and go unnoticed by patients. Which complaint is most characteristic of a patient with a right superior homonymous quadrantanopia?

options.text: Difficulty reading because of central blurring
Repeatedly tripping over objects on the floor to the right
Repeatedly hitting the head on objects above and to the right
Multiple car accidents from vehicles on both sides
Inability to see in dim light after sunset

explanation: Patients with superior quadrantanopia hit their heads on objects above them; those with inferior quadrantanopia bump into or trip over things below; those with bitemporal hemianopia have car accidents from lost peripheral vision.
high_yield_pearl: Superior quad → hits head; inferior quad → trips; bitemporal → car accidents.

source: Content Q4: CN III infarct vs compression
question: A 58-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes has sudden double vision and a droopy right eyelid. His eyes in primary gaze are shown. The right pupil is 3 mm and reacts briskly to light. Which is the most likely cause?

options.text: Lesion of the right sympathetic chain
Ischemic infarct of the right oculomotor nerve
Compression of right CN III by a PComm aneurysm
Infarct of the right abducens nerve
Infarct of the right trochlear nerve

explanation: The figure shows the right eye down and out with ptosis. CN III infarcts (e.g., diabetes, stroke) cause the down-and-out eye, impaired medial gaze, and ptosis, but the pupil is spared because pupillomotor fibers run superficially and are less affected by ischemia. Compression affects these superficial fibers first, causing a dilated pupil.
high_yield_pearl: CN III infarct: down-and-out eye + ptosis, pupil spared. Compression: blown pupil first.

source: Content Q4: CN III compression
question: A 45-year-old woman has the sudden onset of the worst headache of her life. Her eyes in room light are shown. The right pupil does not constrict to direct or consensual light, but eye movements and eyelid position are normal. Which is the most likely cause?

options.text: Ischemic infarct of the right oculomotor nerve
Lesion of the right optic nerve
Compression of right CN III by a PComm aneurysm
Lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Lesion of the right sympathetic chain

explanation: The figure shows a dilated right pupil (mydriasis) with normal eye position. Compression of CN III (posterior communicating artery aneurysm, uncal herniation) first affects the superficial parasympathetic fibers, producing a dilated, unreactive pupil while eye movements remain normal. A right optic nerve lesion would still allow consensual constriction of the right pupil.
high_yield_pearl: PComm aneurysm/uncal herniation compresses CN III → fixed dilated pupil, eye movements normal.

source: Lecture slides 32-33: Uncal herniation
question: A 32-year-old man has an expanding right temporal epidural hematoma after a motorcycle crash. As the uncus herniates over the tentorial edge, which ocular finding is most likely to appear first?

options.text: Bilateral vertical gaze palsy
Left eye unable to adduct
Constricted right pupil with ptosis
Right eye deviated medially
Fixed, dilated right pupil

explanation: Uncal herniation compresses the ipsilateral CN III. Compression impairs the pupillary light reflex (parasympathetic fibers on the outside of the nerve) before it affects the extraocular muscles, producing a fixed, dilated pupil on the side of the lesion.
high_yield_pearl: Uncal herniation → ipsilateral blown pupil (CN III compression).

source: Lecture slide 10: CN IV palsy
question: A 30-year-old man has vertical double vision after striking his head in a fall. Diplopia is worst when he walks down stairs, and he keeps his head tilted toward his left shoulder. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.text: Right trochlear nerve
Left oculomotor nerve
Right oculomotor nerve
Left trochlear nerve
Right abducens nerve

explanation: CN IV innervates the superior oblique, which moves the eye down and in. Loss causes difficulty looking down and medially (e.g., descending stairs). Patients tilt the head AWAY from the affected side to compensate, so a left head tilt indicates a right CN IV palsy.
high_yield_pearl: CN IV palsy: trouble looking down and in; head tilts away from the lesion.

source: Lecture slides 11-12: CN VI palsy
question: A 60-year-old woman reports horizontal double vision that worsens when she looks toward her right. Her eyes in primary gaze are shown. Which nerve is most likely affected?

options.text: Right oculomotor nerve
Right trochlear nerve
Left abducens nerve
Right abducens nerve
Right medial longitudinal fasciculus

explanation: The figure shows the right eye deviated medially. CN VI supplies the lateral rectus; when it is lost, the unopposed medial rectus pulls the eye medially, and the eye cannot abduct (diplopia worse on looking toward the lesion).
high_yield_pearl: CN VI palsy: affected eye turned in (unopposed medial rectus).

source: Content Q7: Testing the obliques
question: During a cranial nerve exam, a student wants to isolate the action of the right superior oblique muscle. Which maneuver is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask the patient to look straight down from center
Adduct the eye, then ask the patient to look up
Abduct the eye, then ask the patient to look down
Abduct the eye, then ask the patient to look up
Adduct the eye, then ask the patient to look down

explanation: To test the obliques, move the eye medially and then have the patient look up (inferior oblique) or down (superior oblique). The superior and inferior recti are tested in abduction (abduct then elevate = superior rectus; abduct then depress = inferior rectus).
high_yield_pearl: Obliques are tested in ADduction; recti in ABduction.

source: Lecture slide 6 / Content Q8
question: Which of the following muscles is NOT innervated by the oculomotor nerve (CN III)?

options.text: Levator palpebrae superioris
Inferior rectus
Superior oblique
Medial rectus
Inferior oblique

explanation: CN III innervates the medial, superior, and inferior recti, the inferior oblique, and the levator palpebrae superioris (plus parasympathetics to the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle). CN IV supplies the superior oblique; CN VI supplies the lateral rectus (LR6 SO4).
high_yield_pearl: LR6, SO4, all the rest CN III.

source: Lecture slide 8: Down and out
question: In a complete right oculomotor nerve palsy, the right eye rests in a 'down and out' position. Which unopposed muscles produce this position?

options.text: Superior oblique and lateral rectus
Superior rectus and lateral rectus
Superior oblique and inferior rectus
Inferior oblique and medial rectus
Inferior rectus and medial rectus

explanation: With CN III lost, the only remaining extraocular muscles are the superior oblique (CN IV; depresses) and lateral rectus (CN VI; abducts). Like a tug of war, the intact muscles pull the eye down and out.
high_yield_pearl: Down and out = unopposed SO (CN IV) + LR (CN VI).

source: Lecture slide 14 / Content Q2: Dilation pathway
question: The pupillary dilation pathway is a three-neuron sympathetic chain. Where are the cell bodies of the first-order (central) neurons located?

options.text: Ciliary ganglion
Intermediolateral cell column
Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Hypothalamus
Superior cervical ganglion

explanation: 1st-order: hypothalamus → hypothalamospinal fibers in the lateral brainstem (neighbors of the ALS). 2nd-order: intermediolateral cell column (preganglionic) → sympathetic chain. 3rd-order: superior cervical ganglion → internal carotid plexus → long ciliary nerves → pupillary dilator.
high_yield_pearl: Dilation: hypothalamus → IML (T1-L3) → superior cervical ganglion → dilator pupillae.

source: Lecture slides 16-17: Preganglionic neurons
question: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons that ultimately control the pupillary dilator muscle have their cell bodies in which location?

options.text: Ciliary ganglion in the posterior orbit
Intermediolateral cell column of the upper thoracic cord
Pretectal nucleus of the rostral midbrain
Ventral horn of the lower cervical cord
Superior cervical ganglion in the neck

explanation: Hypothalamospinal fibers terminate on preganglionic sympathetic neurons in the lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column, T1-L3). Their axons exit in ventral roots, pass through white rami communicantes, and ascend the sympathetic chain to the superior cervical ganglion.
high_yield_pearl: 2nd-order (preganglionic) sympathetic neurons = IML cell column, lateral horn.

source: Content Q2: Horner and the internal carotid
question: A 38-year-old woman develops left-sided neck pain after chiropractic manipulation. The next day she notices a slightly droopy left eyelid and a small left pupil. Imaging shows a dissection of the vessel carrying the postganglionic pupillodilator fibers. Which vessel is involved?

options.text: Internal carotid artery
Vertebral artery
External carotid artery
Ophthalmic vein
Posterior communicating artery

explanation: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion travel on the internal carotid artery (carotid plexus) into the cranial cavity to reach the dilator pupillae and superior tarsal muscle. Carotid dissection therefore produces ipsilateral Horner syndrome.
high_yield_pearl: Carotid dissection → ipsilateral Horner (postganglionic fibers ride the ICA).

source: Lecture slides 20-21 / Content Q2: Pancoast tumor
question: A 64-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history has right shoulder pain. His eyes in dim light are shown; his right forehead is dry. Chest imaging shows a mass at the apex of the right lung. Compression of which structure explains his eye findings?

options.text: Right abducens nerve
Right oculomotor nerve
Right ciliary ganglion
Cervical sympathetic chain
Right optic nerve

explanation: The figure shows mild right ptosis and miosis; together with anhidrosis this is Horner syndrome. The peripheral sympathetic route passes over the lung apex in the sympathetic chain, where a Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumor can compress it.
high_yield_pearl: Pancoast tumor → sympathetic chain → ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis.

source: Case 4: Lateral brainstem lesion
question: A neurology resident shows you an MRI with a small infarct in the lateral brainstem on the RIGHT side. The patient has ptosis of the right eye and a constricted right pupil. Which additional deficit is this patient most likely to have?

options.text: Weakness of the left arm and leg
Loss of pain and temperature on the right side of the body
Loss of pain and temperature on the left side of the body
Right homonymous hemianopia
Paralysis of vertical gaze

explanation: Descending hypothalamospinal (pupillodilator) fibers travel in the lateral brainstem as neighbors of the anterolateral system (ALS). The ALS has already crossed in the spinal cord, so a right lateral brainstem lesion causes right Horner syndrome plus loss of pain and temperature on the LEFT body.
high_yield_pearl: Lateral brainstem: ipsilateral Horner + contralateral body pain/temp loss (ALS neighbor).

source: Lecture slide 19: Superior tarsal muscle
question: Ptosis in Horner syndrome is mild compared with the complete ptosis of an oculomotor palsy. Paralysis of which muscle causes the ptosis in Horner syndrome?

options.text: Levator palpebrae superioris
Superior tarsal (Müller) muscle
Frontalis
Orbicularis oculi
Superior rectus

explanation: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers innervate the superior tarsal muscle, which helps raise the upper eyelid; its loss causes mild ptosis. The levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) is the main elevator, so CN III palsy causes more severe ptosis.
high_yield_pearl: Horner ptosis = superior tarsal muscle (sympathetic); CN III ptosis = levator.

source: Content Q3: Autonomic transmitters
question: A topical drug produces pupillary constriction by directly activating receptors on the sphincter pupillae. Which receptor is the drug stimulating?

options.text: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor
Beta-2 adrenergic receptor
Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
Dopamine D2 receptor
Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor

explanation: Pupillary constriction is parasympathetic: ACh acting on muscarinic receptors of the sphincter pupillae (postganglionic fibers from the ciliary ganglion). Pupillary dilation is sympathetic: norepinephrine acting on adrenergic (alpha-1) receptors of the dilator pupillae.
high_yield_pearl: Constriction = parasympathetic, ACh/muscarinic. Dilation = sympathetic, NE/adrenergic.

source: Lecture slide 23: Light reflex afferents
question: Retinal ganglion cell axons that mediate the pupillary light reflex leave the main visual pathway before reaching the thalamus. By which route do they reach their midbrain target?

options.text: Lateral geniculate nucleus to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Meyer's loop to the inferior colliculus
Posterior commissure directly to the ciliary ganglion
Optic radiations to the cuneus and lingual gyrus
Brachium of the superior colliculus to the pretectal nucleus

explanation: Light reflex fibers travel in the optic nerve, chiasm, and tract but do NOT synapse in the LGN. They use the brachium of the superior colliculus to synapse in the pretectal nucleus in the rostral midbrain.
high_yield_pearl: Light reflex: optic tract → brachium of SC → pretectal nucleus (bypasses LGN).

source: Lecture slide 25: Consensual response
question: Shining light into one eye normally causes constriction of both pupils. Which anatomical feature is primarily responsible for the consensual response?

options.text: Optic radiation fibers cross in the corpus callosum
The MLF links the two oculomotor nuclei
Pretectal neurons project bilaterally to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei
Edinger-Westphal axons cross within the oculomotor nerve
The ciliary ganglion projects to both pupillary sphincters

explanation: Each pretectal nucleus projects to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, with crossing fibers in the posterior commissure. Because of this bilateral (redundant) projection, light in one eye activates both CN IIIs.
high_yield_pearl: Pretectal nucleus → BOTH Edinger-Westphal nuclei (via posterior commissure) = consensual response.

source: Lecture slide 25-26: Efferent limb
question: Preganglionic parasympathetic axons from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus travel in CN III. Where do they synapse, and how do the postganglionic fibers reach the pupillary sphincter?

options.text: Otic ganglion; auriculotemporal nerve
Superior cervical ganglion; long ciliary nerves
Pterygopalatine ganglion; zygomatic nerve
Ciliary ganglion; short ciliary nerves
Ciliary ganglion; long ciliary nerves

explanation: EW preganglionic fibers travel in CN III and synapse in the ciliary ganglion; postganglionic fibers travel in the short ciliary nerves to the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle. Sympathetic dilator fibers use the long ciliary nerves.
high_yield_pearl: Parasympathetic: EW → CN III → ciliary ganglion → SHORT ciliary nerves.

source: Content Q5 table: Optic nerve lesion
question: A patient has a complete lesion of the right optic nerve. When a penlight is shone into the RIGHT eye, which response is expected?

options.text: Only the left pupil constricts
Neither pupil constricts
Only the right pupil constricts
The right pupil constricts and the left dilates
Both pupils constrict normally

explanation: The optic nerve is the afferent limb. With the right optic nerve cut, light in the right eye reaches neither pretectal nucleus, so there is no direct (right) or consensual (left) response. Light in the left eye produces normal constriction of both pupils.
high_yield_pearl: Afferent (CN II) lesion: light in that eye → no direct and no consensual response.

source: Content Q5 table: CN III lesion
question: A patient has a complete lesion of the right oculomotor nerve. When a penlight is shone into the LEFT eye, which response is expected?

options.text: Left pupil constricts; right pupil does not
Both pupils dilate
Neither pupil constricts
Right pupil constricts; left pupil does not
Both pupils constrict normally

explanation: CN III is the efferent limb. Light in the left eye is sensed normally and both EW nuclei are activated, so the left pupil constricts (direct), but the right pupil cannot constrict because its efferent nerve is cut (absent consensual). Light in the right eye would produce a left consensual response but no right direct response.
high_yield_pearl: Efferent (CN III) lesion: that pupil never constricts, whichever eye is lit.

source: Content Q5: Optic tract lesion and light reflex
question: A 52-year-old man has a lesion of the right optic tract causing left homonymous hemianopia. What is the expected effect on the pupillary light reflex?

options.text: Absent direct responses bilaterally
Absent responses when light is shone in the left eye
Normal direct and consensual responses in both eyes
Absent responses when light is shone in the right eye
Absent consensual responses bilaterally

explanation: Each eye projects to both optic tracts and to the midbrain reflex center bilaterally. The remaining (left) optic tract still carries input from both eyes to the pretectal area, and the pretectal nuclei project bilaterally, so responses remain normal. Lesions of the optic radiations, posterior commissure, or LGN likewise leave the reflex intact.
high_yield_pearl: Only CN II or CN III lesions abolish the light reflex; most central lesions don't (redundancy).

source: Content Q6: LGN lesion and accommodation
question: A patient has a lesion of the right lateral geniculate nucleus. When asked to follow a finger moving toward her nose, how will accommodation be affected?

options.text: Absent convergence with normal pupil constriction
Absent accommodation in the left eye only
Absent accommodation in the right eye only
Absent accommodation in both eyes
Normal accommodation in both eyes

explanation: Although information is blocked to the right visual cortex, the left visual cortex still receives input and activates the left pretectal area, which distributes signals to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei. Accommodation therefore occurs normally.
high_yield_pearl: Unilateral LGN or radiation lesions spare accommodation (bilateral midbrain distribution).

source: Case 3: Occipital trauma
question: After a fall onto his occiput, a 25-year-old man has extensive destruction of both occipital lobes and is completely blind. Which finding is most likely on examination of his pupils?

options.text: Fixed dilated pupils in both eyes
Normal pupillary light reflexes in both eyes
Absent light reflexes with intact accommodation
Absent light reflexes in both eyes
Argyll Robertson pupils in both eyes

explanation: The pupillary light reflex uses optic nerve → optic tract → pretectal area → EW nucleus, bypassing the occipital cortex, so it is normal. Accommodation to an approaching finger cannot be elicited (he cannot see it), but voluntary convergence still produces pupil constriction.
high_yield_pearl: Cortical blindness: light reflex intact; accommodation to visual target lost.

source: Lecture slides 34-36: Accommodation
question: When a person shifts gaze from a distant mountain to read text held close to the face, the accommodation response occurs. Which three changes make up this response?

options.text: Conjugate lateral gaze, constriction, and lens flattening
Convergence, pupillary dilation, and lens rounding
Divergence, pupillary dilation, and lens flattening
Convergence, pupillary constriction, and lens rounding
Divergence, pupillary constriction, and lens flattening

explanation: Accommodation (near response): the eyes converge (oculomotor nucleus → medial recti), the pupils constrict, and the lens rounds (EW nucleus → ciliary muscle contraction). It uses retina → visual cortex → midbrain reflex center.
high_yield_pearl: Near triad: convergence + miosis + lens rounding.

source: Lecture slide 37: Argyll Robertson pupil
question: A 55-year-old man with a history of untreated syphilis has small, irregular pupils that do not constrict to bright light but constrict briskly when he focuses on a near object. Where is the lesion most likely located?

options.text: Pretectal area of the midbrain
Optic nerve
Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Oculomotor nerve
Ciliary ganglion

explanation: Argyll Robertson pupils ('accommodate but do not react') occur in neurosyphilis and diabetes. The lesion is probably in the pretectal area, which contains separate populations of neurons for light-evoked and accommodation-evoked constriction. Lesions of EW, CN III, or the ciliary ganglion would abolish both responses.
high_yield_pearl: Argyll Robertson: no light response, intact near response; syphilis/diabetes; pretectal lesion.

source: Lecture slides 39-40 / Content Q10: Parinaud
question: A 14-year-old boy has morning headaches and cannot look upward. MRI shows a mass in the pineal region compressing the dorsal midbrain. Damage to which structure best explains his gaze deficit?

options.text: Paramedian pontine reticular formation
Optic chiasm
Medial longitudinal fasciculus
Abducens nucleus
Posterior commissure

explanation: The vertical gaze center lies in the midbrain, and its axons cross through the posterior commissure. Pinealomas and posterior midbrain infarcts disrupt the posterior commissure, causing vertical gaze paralysis (Parinaud syndrome).
high_yield_pearl: Pinealoma → posterior commissure → vertical gaze palsy (Parinaud).

source: Lecture slide 43: FEF stimulation
question: During awake brain surgery, a neurosurgeon electrically stimulates the LEFT frontal eye field. Which eye movement is most likely to occur?

options.text: Both eyes move to the right
Only the right eye abducts
Both eyes move upward
Both eyes move to the left
Only the left eye adducts

explanation: Each FEF sends axons to the contralateral PPRF (horizontal gaze center). Activating the left FEF activates the right PPRF, which drives the right lateral rectus (via CN VI) and the left medial rectus (via the MLF and CN III), so both eyes move to the right.
high_yield_pearl: FEF drives gaze to the OPPOSITE side.

source: Content Q11: FEF stroke rule
question: A 70-year-old man has an acute infarct of the right frontal eye field. In which direction are his eyes most likely deviated?

options.text: Left eye laterally only
Right eye medially only
Both eyes toward the right
Both eyes upward
Both eyes toward the left

explanation: Normally the two FEFs are balanced. A right FEF infarct leaves the left FEF unopposed, which drives the eyes to the right. Rule: with a stroke the eyes look TOWARD the lesion (and away from the hemiparesis).
high_yield_pearl: FEF stroke: eyes look toward the lesion.

source: Content Q11: FEF seizure rule
question: A 22-year-old woman has a focal seizure arising in the right frontal eye field. During the seizure, in which direction are her eyes most likely deviated?

options.text: Right eye laterally only
Left eye medially only
Both eyes downward
Both eyes toward the left
Both eyes toward the right

explanation: Seizure activity increases the output of the right FEF, which drives the contralateral (left) PPRF, turning both eyes to the left. Rule: with a seizure the eyes look AWAY from the lesion.
high_yield_pearl: FEF seizure: eyes look away from the focus.

source: Case 2: Eyes fixed to the left
question: You are called to the ED to evaluate a patient whose eyes are both fixed in position looking to her LEFT. Which single lesion could account for this finding?

options.text: Lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Infarct of the right PPRF
Infarct of the right frontal eye field
Infarct of the left PPRF
Seizure focus in the left frontal eye field

explanation: A right PPRF lesion leaves the left PPRF dominant, turning both eyes to the left (paralysis of right gaze). The same leftward deviation could result from a LEFT FEF infarct or a RIGHT FEF seizure. A right FEF infarct, left FEF seizure, or left PPRF lesion would turn the eyes to the right; a left MLF lesion causes INO.
high_yield_pearl: PPRF lesion: eyes deviate AWAY from the lesion (paralysis of gaze toward it).

source: Case 1: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
question: A 28-year-old woman with a 3-year history of multiple sclerosis reports double vision when she looks to her left. Gaze to the right is normal. Her attempted leftward gaze is shown. Where is the lesion?

options.text: Right paramedian pontine reticular formation
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Right medial longitudinal fasciculus
Right abducens nucleus
Left frontal eye field

explanation: The figure shows the left eye abducting normally while the right eye stays midline on leftward gaze. The left PPRF/abducens nucleus sends signals through the RIGHT MLF to the right oculomotor nucleus (medial rectus). A right MLF lesion prevents right eye adduction: right internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
high_yield_pearl: INO is named for the side of the eye that fails to adduct = side of the MLF lesion.

source: Case 1B / Lecture slide 46: INO and convergence
question: In the patient with a right MLF lesion, the physician tests accommodation by having her follow a finger toward her nose. What will most likely be observed, and why?

options.text: Absent lens rounding, because the EW nucleus is lesioned
Absent pupillary constriction, because CN III is damaged
Absent right eye adduction, because the MLF carries convergence
Normal convergence, because the near pathway bypasses the pons
Divergence of both eyes, because the PPRF is disinhibited

explanation: Accommodation travels from the visual cortex to the midbrain pretectal area and oculomotor nucleus, bypassing the pons and MLF. CN III can be activated by multiple pathways, so the right eye adducts normally during convergence even though it fails during lateral gaze.
high_yield_pearl: INO: adduction fails on lateral gaze but is preserved during convergence.

source: Lecture slides 41-42: MLF
question: Conjugate horizontal gaze requires the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). Which connection does the MLF provide?

options.text: Vertical gaze center to contralateral CN III
Abducens nucleus to contralateral oculomotor nucleus
Pretectal nucleus to Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Oculomotor nucleus to ipsilateral trochlear nucleus
Frontal eye field to contralateral PPRF

explanation: The PPRF in the caudal pons activates the ipsilateral abducens nucleus. Abducens internuclear neurons send axons through the contralateral MLF to the oculomotor nucleus (medial rectus) so that both eyes move together. FEF → contralateral PPRF fibers are cortical, not MLF.
high_yield_pearl: MLF: CN VI nucleus → contralateral CN III nucleus (medial rectus) for conjugate lateral gaze.

source: Case 5: Cavernous sinus thrombosis
question: A 47-year-old man has 6 days of headache, upper facial pain, fever, and a swollen, closed left eye that began after a toothache with gum swelling. The left eye is proptotic, cannot move in any direction, has an absent corneal reflex, and a sluggish pupil. MRI shows a dilated cavernous sinus and superior ophthalmic vein. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Pituitary adenoma with apoplexy
Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis

explanation: CN III, IV, VI, V1, and V2 travel in the cavernous sinus, which receives the valveless superior and inferior ophthalmic veins. Dental or sinus infection can spread to the sinus, causing thrombosis with ophthalmoplegia, absent corneal reflex (V1), proptosis, and fever. It requires urgent treatment because infection can spread to the brain.
high_yield_pearl: Cavernous sinus: CN III, IV, VI, V1, V2 (+ ICA); fed by valveless ophthalmic veins.

source: Case 5 / Content Q9: Cavernous sinus contents
question: In the patient with cavernous sinus thrombosis, involvement of which nerve best explains the absent corneal reflex on the left?

options.text: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1)
Optic nerve (CN II)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
Abducens nerve (CN VI)

explanation: The afferent limb of the corneal reflex is V1 (nasociliary branch), which passes through the cavernous sinus. The efferent limb is CN VII, which is not in the sinus. CN III and VI involvement explains the ophthalmoplegia and sluggish pupil.
high_yield_pearl: Corneal reflex: afferent V1 (in cavernous sinus), efferent CN VII.

source: Content Q12: Types of eye movements
question: A patient fixates on a stationary target on the wall while the examiner briskly rotates the patient's head to the right. The patient's eyes move to the left so that fixation is maintained. Which type of eye movement is this?

options.text: Saccade
Accommodation
Smooth pursuit
Vestibulo-ocular reflex
Vergence

explanation: In the vestibulo-ocular reflex, head movement causes the eyes to move in the opposite direction to keep a stationary object fixed. Saccades move fixation from one stationary object to another; smooth pursuit tracks a moving object; vergence moves the eyes in opposite directions.
high_yield_pearl: VOR: eyes move opposite to the head to stay on target.

source: Lecture: Microphthalmos slide 3
question: A newborn has a noticeably small left eye. Examination shows a disorganized globe with malformed internal structures. Which term best describes this condition?

options.text: Coloboma
Aniridia
Congenital glaucoma
Nanophthalmos
Microphthalmos

explanation: Microphthalmos is a small, disorganized eye, and vision is always affected; severity ranges from mild to anophthalmia. Nanophthalmos is a small eye with normal internal structure.
high_yield_pearl: Microphthalmos = small + disorganized; nanophthalmos = small + normally structured.

source: Lecture: Microphthalmos slide 4
question: A 2-month-old infant has mild unilateral microphthalmos of the right eye with potential for useful vision. Which management step is most important to preserve vision in the affected eye?

options.text: Patching of the better eye to treat amblyopia
Immediate enucleation of the small eye
No intervention until adolescence
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection
Topical prostaglandin analog drops

explanation: Unilateral microphthalmos will invariably cause amblyopia, because unbalanced input during the critical period impairs cortical development. Patching the better eye forces use of the affected eye. Management otherwise depends on associated cataract, glaucoma, retinal detachment, or corneal opacity.
high_yield_pearl: Unilateral congenital eye disease → amblyopia → patch the good eye.

source: Lecture: Coloboma slide 5
question: A 1-year-old has a 'keyhole'-shaped pupil in the left eye extending inferiorly. Fundoscopy shows a similar defect involving the inferior retina and choroid. Which developmental error caused this?

options.text: VEGF-driven abnormal retinal vessel growth
Failure of the optic (choroidal) fissure to close
Mutation of PAX6 with absent iris tissue
Malformation of the trabecular meshwork
Persistence of the fetal pupillary membrane

explanation: Coloboma results from failure of the embryonic optic fissure to close. It often appears only as a keyhole iris defect but can involve the ciliary body, lens, choroid, retina, or optic disc, with or without anterior involvement.
high_yield_pearl: Coloboma = failed optic fissure closure → keyhole defect.

source: Lecture: Aniridia slide 7
question: A 2-year-old boy with no family history of eye disease has near-total absence of the iris in both eyes, nystagmus, and poor vision. Genetic testing shows a PAX6 deletion. Which additional evaluation is most important?

options.text: Urine catecholamines for neuroblastoma
Fundoscopy to screen for retinoblastoma only
Serial renal ultrasound to screen for Wilms tumor
Plasma metanephrines for pheochromocytoma
MRI of the brain for medulloblastoma

explanation: Aniridia is caused by PAX6 mutations (usually autosomal dominant). Non-familial (sporadic) cases are associated with WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability), so renal screening is needed. Aniridia also causes foveal hypoplasia (nystagmus), glaucoma (~50%), cataract, and corneal opacification.
high_yield_pearl: Sporadic aniridia (PAX6) → WAGR → screen for Wilms tumor.

source: Lecture slides 8-9 / Content Q1: Congenital glaucoma
question: A 4-month-old girl has excessive tearing, sensitivity to light, and frequent squeezing of her eyelids. Both corneas are enlarged and hazy. Which is the most appropriate diagnosis and treatment?

options.text: Retinopathy of prematurity; anti-VEGF injection
Bacterial conjunctivitis; topical antibiotics
Congenital glaucoma; urgent goniotomy or trabeculotomy
Congenital cataract; observation until age 2
Nasolacrimal duct obstruction; lacrimal sac massage

explanation: The classic triad of congenital glaucoma is tearing, photophobia, and blepharospasm. Malformation of the trabecular meshwork impairs aqueous outflow; the distensible infant eye enlarges under high IOP. It is universally blinding if untreated and needs urgent surgery that cuts through the trabecular meshwork.
high_yield_pearl: Congenital glaucoma: tearing + photophobia + blepharospasm; enlarged eye; urgent goniotomy/trabeculotomy.

source: Lecture slides 10-11 / Content Q1: ROP
question: A boy born at 26 weeks' gestation weighing 800 g undergoes eye screening in the NICU. Which process underlies the disease being screened for?

options.text: Separation of the neural retina from the pigment epithelium
VEGF-driven abnormal vessels at the vascular-avascular retinal border
Inflammatory cells accumulating in the anterior chamber
Failure of closure of the embryonic optic fissure
Deposition of drusen beneath the retinal pigment epithelium

explanation: Retinopathy of prematurity: damaged fetal retinal vessels induce VEGF release, producing abnormal, defective vessel growth at the border of vascular and avascular retina. It is graded by zone and stage; most cases resolve, and treatment is anti-VEGF injection or laser.
high_yield_pearl: ROP: VEGF-driven neovascularization in premature infants; treat with anti-VEGF or laser.

source: Lecture slide 10: ROP screening criteria
question: Which of the following infants meets the criteria for retinopathy of prematurity screening?

options.text: Born at 34 weeks' gestation weighing 2,000 g
Born at 38 weeks' gestation weighing 3,100 g
Born at 33 weeks' gestation weighing 1,900 g
Born at 36 weeks' gestation weighing 2,400 g
Born at 29 weeks' gestation weighing 1,350 g

explanation: Infants born before 31 weeks and weighing less than 1,500 g need ROP screening. Most infants with treatable disease are about 26 weeks and 800 g. ROP treatment is among the most cost-effective treatments in medicine.
high_yield_pearl: Screen for ROP: <31 weeks and <1,500 g.

source: Content Q1: Persistent pupillary membrane
question: A newborn has fine strands of tissue stretching across the pupil of the right eye that partially obscure the visual axis. Which developmental explanation is most likely?

options.text: Malformation of the trabecular meshwork
Absence of iris tissue from PAX6 mutation
Abnormal retinal vessel growth from VEGF
Failure of the fetal pupillary membrane to atrophy
Failure of closure of the optic fissure

explanation: A persistent pupillary membrane is a fetal membrane that fails to atrophy after birth and covers the pupil. It is treated surgically when it obstructs vision.
high_yield_pearl: Persistent pupillary membrane = fetal membrane fails to regress; surgery if it blocks the pupil.

source: Lecture slide 13: Definition of glaucoma
question: Which statement best defines glaucoma?

options.text: A progressive optic neuropathy with cupping of the optic nerve
An inflammation of the uveal tract of the eye
A degeneration of the macula with drusen deposits
Any elevation of intraocular pressure above normal
A clouding of the natural crystalline lens

explanation: Glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy manifested by cupping of the optic nerve. About 90% of cases are associated with high IOP, and IOP is the only modifiable risk factor; all treatments (drops, laser, surgery) aim to lower it.
high_yield_pearl: Glaucoma = optic nerve cupping; IOP is the only modifiable risk factor.

source: Lecture slide 15: Glaucoma physiology
question: An ophthalmologist explains that no eye disease is caused by oversecretion of aqueous humor and that all glaucoma is a drainage problem. Through which structure does aqueous humor normally drain?

options.text: Nonpigmented ciliary body epithelium
Trabecular meshwork at the iridocorneal angle
Bruch membrane into the choroid
Optic disc into the subarachnoid space
Vitreous body and central retinal vein

explanation: Aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary body (behind the iris), circulates to the anterior chamber, and drains via the trabecular meshwork at the iridocorneal angle (with a smaller uveoscleral pathway).
high_yield_pearl: Ciliary body produces aqueous; trabecular meshwork drains it.

source: Lecture slides 16-17 / Content Q2: POAG
question: A 62-year-old African American man has a routine eye exam. He has no symptoms. IOP is elevated, the optic discs show increased cupping, and visual field testing shows peripheral field loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Wet age-related macular degeneration
Nuclear cataract
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Primary open-angle glaucoma

explanation: Chronic open-angle glaucoma is asymptomatic and causes painless loss of peripheral vision, so screening is essential. It is the most common glaucoma in the USA, and people of African descent have 6-8 times the rate of Caucasians with higher rates of blindness.
high_yield_pearl: POAG: painless, asymptomatic peripheral loss; screen; higher in people of African descent.

source: Case 2A / Content Q2: Angle-closure glaucoma
question: A 55-year-old woman comes to the ED with a severely painful left eye, headache, and nausea that began after she walked into a dark movie theater. She sees halos around lights. The left eye is red with a fixed, mid-dilated pupil, and it feels rock hard to palpation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Retinal detachment
Bacterial conjunctivitis
Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Migraine with visual aura
Acute anterior uveitis

explanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with a red, painful eye, headache, nausea/vomiting, halos, sudden vision change, and a mid-dilated fixed pupil. Dim light dilates the pupil, causing pupillary block and obstruction of the iridocorneal angle with a sudden rise in IOP. It is an emergency.
high_yield_pearl: Red painful eye + halos + mid-dilated pupil + rock-hard globe after dim light = acute angle closure.

source: Lecture slide 17: AACG epidemiology
question: Which patient is at the greatest risk of developing acute angle-closure glaucoma?

options.text: A 58-year-old woman with hyperopia (farsightedness)
A 75-year-old man after cataract surgery
A 22-year-old man with high myopia
A 3-year-old child with aniridia
A 30-year-old woman with astigmatism

explanation: Acute angle closure classically affects middle-aged hyperopes: short eyes have a crowded anterior segment and narrow angle. Chronic angle closure is more common in East Asian populations, while POAG predominates in the USA.
high_yield_pearl: Acute angle closure = middle-aged hyperope (short eye, narrow angle).

source: Content Q3: Pupil size and outflow
question: Why does entering a darkened room precipitate an attack in a patient with a narrow iridocorneal angle?

options.text: Darkness causes the lens to dislocate forward
Darkness increases secretion by the ciliary body
Dim light stimulates choroidal neovascularization
Pupillary dilation crowds the iris into the drainage angle
Dim light causes hemorrhage into the vitreous

explanation: Pupillary dilation bunches the peripheral iris into the iridocorneal angle and promotes pupillary block, so aqueous is trapped behind the iris (iris bombé) and outflow is blocked. Constriction pulls the iris away from the angle, widens the trabecular meshwork, and increases outflow.
high_yield_pearl: Dilation closes the angle; constriction opens it.

source: Content Q3: Drugs and angle closure
question: A 60-year-old hyperopic woman with known narrow angles is about to receive an eye drop before a fundus exam. Which drug is most likely to precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma?

options.text: Pilocarpine
Brimonidine
Timolol
Atropine
Latanoprost

explanation: Antimuscarinic mydriatics such as atropine dilate the pupil and can close a narrow angle. Pilocarpine (a cholinomimetic) constricts the pupil and opens the angle. Timolol, latanoprost, and brimonidine lower IOP.
high_yield_pearl: Avoid mydriatics (e.g., atropine) in narrow angles.

source: Content Q3-4: Cholinomimetics
question: Pilocarpine is used in the management of angle-closure glaucoma. Which statement best describes its mechanism and a characteristic adverse effect?

options.text: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that increases outflow; causes ptosis
Muscarinic agonist that increases outflow; causes cyclospasm
Beta-blocker that decreases synthesis; causes mydriasis
Alpha-2 agonist that decreases synthesis; causes pruritus
Prostaglandin analog that increases outflow; causes miosis

explanation: Cholinomimetics such as pilocarpine activate muscarinic receptors, constricting the pupil and contracting the ciliary muscle. This pulls the iris from the angle and opens the trabecular meshwork, increasing outflow. Adverse effects: cyclospasm (ciliary muscle spasm) and miosis.
high_yield_pearl: Pilocarpine: ↑ outflow via miosis; AE = cyclospasm, miosis.

source: Content Q4: Prostaglandin analogs
question: A 66-year-old woman being treated for open-angle glaucoma notices that her eyelashes have grown noticeably longer and darker since she started a nightly eye drop. How does this drug lower intraocular pressure?

options.text: Reduces ocular inflammation via steroid receptors
Decreases aqueous synthesis via beta-receptor blockade
Decreases aqueous synthesis via alpha-2 agonism
Decreases aqueous synthesis via carbonic anhydrase inhibition
Increases outflow of aqueous humor

explanation: Prostaglandin analogs (e.g., latanoprost) increase aqueous humor outflow (uveoscleral pathway). Their characteristic adverse effect is eyelash growth (also iris darkening).
high_yield_pearl: Prostaglandin analogs: ↑ outflow; AE = eyelash growth.

source: Content Q4: Beta blockers
question: A topical beta-blocker such as timolol is prescribed for open-angle glaucoma. By what mechanism does it lower intraocular pressure?

options.text: Decreases aqueous humor production by the ciliary body
Constricts the pupil to open the drainage angle
Creates a channel to a subconjunctival bleb
Reduces inflammation of the trabecular meshwork
Increases uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor

explanation: Beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (diuretics) all decrease secretion of aqueous by the ciliary body. Prostaglandins and cholinomimetics increase outflow. (Clinically, systemic absorption can worsen asthma or bradycardia.)
high_yield_pearl: Decrease production: β-blockers, α2-agonists, CA inhibitors. Increase outflow: prostaglandins, cholinomimetics.

source: Content Q4: Alpha agonists
question: Two weeks after starting a new glaucoma drop that decreases aqueous humor synthesis, a patient reports itchy eyes and intermittently blurred vision. Which drug class is most likely responsible?

options.text: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
Cholinomimetic
Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist
Beta-adrenergic blocker
Prostaglandin analog

explanation: Alpha-agonists (e.g., brimonidine) decrease aqueous synthesis; their listed adverse effects are blurry vision and ocular pruritus. Prostaglandins cause eyelash growth; cholinomimetics cause cyclospasm and miosis.
high_yield_pearl: α2-agonists: ↓ aqueous synthesis; AE = blurry vision, ocular pruritus.

source: Content Q4: Diuretics (CA inhibitors)
question: Acetazolamide is given orally to a patient with acutely elevated intraocular pressure. What is its mechanism of action in the eye?

options.text: Blocks sodium channels in the trabecular meshwork
Inhibits carbonic anhydrase to decrease aqueous production
Blocks alpha-1 receptors to constrict the pupil
Activates muscarinic receptors to increase outflow
Activates prostaglandin receptors to increase outflow

explanation: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (diuretics) reduce bicarbonate-dependent secretion of aqueous humor by the ciliary body epithelium, decreasing aqueous synthesis.
high_yield_pearl: Acetazolamide (CA inhibitor) ↓ aqueous synthesis.

source: Lecture slides 18-19: Glaucoma surgery
question: A patient with uncontrolled open-angle glaucoma undergoes a trabeculectomy. How does this procedure lower intraocular pressure?

options.text: Replaces the crystalline lens with an implant
Seals retinal tears to restore retinal attachment
Creates direct flow from the anterior chamber to a subconjunctival bleb
Modifies the trabecular meshwork photochemically
Ablates the ciliary body to reduce aqueous production

explanation: Trabeculectomy creates a direct drainage route from the anterior chamber to a subconjunctival bleb. Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) modifies the trabecular meshwork to increase outflow; diode laser decreases ciliary body production; goniotomy bypasses the trabecular meshwork.
high_yield_pearl: Trabeculectomy = AC → subconjunctival bleb.

source: Case 1C / Content Q2: Cataract
question: A 70-year-old man reports slowly worsening vision over several years and halos and glare around headlights when driving at night. He has no eye pain. When you look through the ophthalmoscope, there is no red reflex. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

options.text: Open-angle glaucoma; prostaglandin drops
Wet macular degeneration; anti-VEGF injection
Retinitis pigmentosa; vitamin supplements
Dry macular degeneration; antioxidant vitamins
Cataract; surgical lens replacement

explanation: Cataract is a painless clouding of the lens from denatured, accumulated lens proteins, causing blur, glare (night driving), a myopic shift, and loss of the red reflex. It is the world's most common cause of blindness and the most treatable; surgery replaces the lens with ~98% success.
high_yield_pearl: Cataract: painless blur + glare/halos + absent red reflex; treat with surgery.

source: Case 1C: Infant cataract
question: Why must a dense cataract be treated promptly in a 6-month-old infant, whereas surgery can often be scheduled electively in a 70-year-old?

options.text: Infant lens proteins become toxic to the retina
Infants cannot undergo surgery after their first year
Infant cataracts commonly spread to the optic nerve
Unbalanced input during the critical period causes permanent amblyopia
Infant cataracts rapidly progress to angle-closure glaucoma

explanation: Cortical circuits for processing visual input develop during the first year. Unbalanced or absent input from one eye impairs this development and causes permanent visual deficits (amblyopia), including blindness, even if the cataract is later removed.
high_yield_pearl: Infant visual deprivation → permanent amblyopia; treat early.

source: Case 1A / Content Q2: Dry AMD
question: A 76-year-old woman has gradual distortion of straight lines (metamorphopsia) when reading. Fundoscopy shows multiple yellow deposits in the macula of both eyes, without hemorrhage. Where are these deposits located, and what is the recommended management?

options.text: Between Bruch membrane and the RPE; antioxidant vitamins
Between the retina and vitreous; laser retinopexy
Within the nerve fiber layer; intravitreal anti-VEGF
Within the lens nucleus; cataract surgery
In the anterior chamber; topical steroids

explanation: Dry age-related macular degeneration involves drusen deposited between Bruch membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium. It causes gradual metamorphopsia, then scotomas, then loss of central acuity. Age is the greatest risk factor; management is vitamins and antioxidants.
high_yield_pearl: Dry AMD: drusen between Bruch membrane and RPE; gradual central loss; vitamins/antioxidants.

source: Lecture slide 25 / Content Q2: Wet AMD
question: An 80-year-old man with known dry macular degeneration wakes up with sudden, severe loss of central vision in his right eye. Fundoscopy shows subretinal hemorrhage in the macula. What is the underlying process, and how is it treated?

options.text: Retinal detachment from a tear; scleral buckle
Optic nerve cupping from high IOP; prostaglandins
Lens protein denaturation; cataract extraction
Angle closure from pupillary block; laser iridotomy
Choroidal neovascularization; intravitreal anti-VEGF

explanation: Wet AMD is preceded by dry AMD and can cause acute 'overnight' vision loss from neovascularization with bleeding between Bruch membrane and the RPE. It is the leading reason for intravitreal anti-VEGF injection.
high_yield_pearl: Wet AMD: neovascularization + hemorrhage; sudden central loss; anti-VEGF.

source: Content Q5: Functional effects of AMD
question: A 78-year-old man has advanced macular degeneration in both eyes. Which activity is he most likely to find difficult?

options.text: Navigating a hallway in dim light
Walking around his room without bumping into furniture
Reading small print in a newspaper
Noticing objects on the floor beside him
Detecting movement in his peripheral vision

explanation: AMD destroys central (macular) vision, impairing activities requiring focused vision such as reading, driving, and sewing. Peripheral vision is preserved, so navigation and peripheral motion detection remain relatively intact.
high_yield_pearl: AMD = central loss → reading, driving, sewing; peripheral navigation preserved.

source: Case 2B / Lecture slide 26: Retinal detachment
question: A 63-year-old woman describes seeing flashing lights and numerous new floaters, followed by a painless dark 'curtain' coming down over the vision of her right eye. Why does this condition damage photoreceptors?

options.text: Inflammatory cells infiltrate the anterior chamber
Elevated IOP compresses ganglion cell axons at the disc
Drusen accumulate between Bruch membrane and the RPE
The outer retina loses its choroidal blood supply and RPE support
Denatured lens proteins block light from the retina

explanation: In retinal detachment, the neural retina separates from the retinal pigment epithelium. The outer third of the retina (photoreceptors) depends on attachment to the choroid for blood supply and on the RPE for protein turnover. RRD is often preceded by posterior vitreous detachment; early tears can be lasered, advanced cases need surgery.
high_yield_pearl: Retinal detachment: flashes + floaters + painless curtain; photoreceptors lose choroidal supply.

source: Content Q2/Q6 / Case 1A: Diabetic retinopathy
question: A 54-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has blurry vision and floaters. Fundoscopy shows microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, flame-shaped hemorrhages, and fragile new vessels on the optic disc. What drives the formation of the new vessels?

options.text: Elevated IOP compressing the central retinal vein
Retinal hypoxia inducing VEGF release
Autoimmune destruction of photoreceptors
Genetic loss of retinal pigment epithelium
Drusen deposition stimulating macrophages

explanation: In diabetic retinopathy, capillary contents leak into surrounding tissue (vasogenic edema and hemorrhage), causing hypoxia. Hypoxia induces VEGF and neovascularization with disorganized, defective capillaries that cause further damage. Treatment: glycemic control, laser, anti-VEGF.
high_yield_pearl: Diabetic retinopathy: leakage → hypoxia → VEGF → neovascularization.
